Gravitational Waves

TT-1 is a three-spacecraft laser interferometer on heliocentric orbits, trailing Earth by 20° with 3-million-kilometre arms. It cannot be built on Mars — so the city exhibits it instead: a 1:1 spacecraft with its gold test mass laid open, and a formation display whose breathing motion is integrated orbital dynamics, not hand animation. Every number on this page passed a known-answer gate first.

01

Why gravitational waves, on Mars

A millihertz interferometer needs arms longer than ten thousand planets. The city can't host the instrument — it hosts the understanding of it.

Strain from a supermassive black-hole merger arrives at 10-21: measuring it means resolving picometres across millions of kilometres, which is why TT-1 flies as three free-falling spacecraft in deep space. What stands in the science quarter is the teaching version: a full-scale engineering unit on a display cradle, its instrument bay cut open so the causal chain reads in one glance — telescope barrel → Zerodur optical bench → the 46 mm Au-Pt cube floating in its electrode cage. The cube is the whole story: a mass touching nothing, whose only remaining force is gravity.

Next to it, the formation exhibit compresses the constellation 2×108:1 (1 Gm → 5 m) while keeping the spacecraft bodies 1:1. Six red beams close the triangle the way six heterodyne links close the real interferometer.

02

How 5.1×10-21 is made

One master equation, two budgets feeding it, and real solvers behind every allocation.

The whole design serves Sh(f) = (10/3L²) [POMS + 2(1+cos²(f/f∗)) Pacc/(2πf)4] [1+0.6(f/f∗)²]. Below a millihertz the (2πf)-4 factor means only residual force on the test mass matters — a nine-term parasitic-force budget (gas damping, charge shot noise, patch potentials, magnetics, radiometer, radiation pressure, stiffness coupling, self-gravity) closes at 2.10 fm/s²/√Hz, gated against LISA Pathfinder flight data. At high frequency the optical chain takes over: an eight-term budget closes at 7.48 pm/√Hz per link.

The allocations are not typed in — they are solved for. Zemax ray tracing confirmed the confocal-paraboloid telescope is aberration-free on axis to 1.9×10-10 waves; a COMSOL→Zemax thermo-elastic loop turned "3 pm of telescope pathlength" into material law (Zerodur survives at 220 µK/√Hz where aluminium needs an impossible 0.19 µK/√Hz); and a self-built two-beam overlap integral put the tilt-to-length coupling on a moment-integral footing, softening the alignment tolerance from 6.25 to 10.7 µm.

03

Five known-answer gates

No home-built model was allowed to speak about the design before reproducing something the world already knows.

GateReproducedVerdict
Sensitivity master equation LISA public curve: f∗ = 19.09 mHz; asymptotic slopes −3 / −2 / +1 pass
Waveform & SNR machinery aLIGO BNS range 220 vs ~190 Mpc; fISCO(2.8 M☉) 1570 vs 1571 Hz; DL(z=1) to 0.03% pass
Optical link LISA received power: 297 pW vs ~300 pW public pass
Constellation dynamics LISA orbital elements e=0.0048, i=0.48°; 60.00° plane tilt emerges from i=√3e pass
Acceleration-noise model LISA Pathfinder in-flight band 1.2–2.5 fm/s²/√Hz pass, flagged weak — spectral shape not reproduced below 1 mHz, so a 2.0 fm/s² unmodelled reserve is carried

The same discipline runs deeper than these five: the FEM was gated on the exact stress-free solution of a linear thermal field (hit to 0.00–0.47%), the wave-optics overlap on a closed-form complex-Gaussian integral (0.00%), and the transmit-aperture efficiency on the literature optimum 0.81 at w=0.89R — reproduced as 0.8145 at 0.890R. A gate that passes too easily is itself a finding: one gate window had to be widened after it was caught hiding a real bug (see 06).

04

Breathing from real orbits

The exhibit's motion loop is a baked year of Sun + Earth-perturbation integration — 1.29% arm breathing, 0.21° yaw wobble, zero keyframes.

Three spacecraft on one shared semi-major axis, eccentricity and inclination vectors rotated 120° apart with i = √3 e: the first-order relative orbit is a circle, so the triangle stays equilateral — and the 60° tilt of its plane is algebra, not a choice. Earth then spoils the ideal: a DOP853 propagation with Earth's point mass shows the formation destroyed at 0° trailing (274% arm flexing) and settling to 2.13% at 20° — the trailing angle is a stability-versus-comm-distance compromise you can read straight off the scan.

The display asset samples year two of that propagation into 120 frames, blends the tail into the head for a closed 36 s loop, and drives each craft's yaw along the baked arm-bisector. Any time offset is a valid entry point; three instances could run phase-shifted. What you see wobbling above the regolith is the actual celestial mechanics that caps the arm length of every space interferometer.

06

What broke

A two-agent independent review corrected fourteen defects. Four of them are worth retelling.

A fit parameter copied 105× too small — and the gate that covered for it

The galactic-foreground fit's κ and γ went in as 0.00521 and 0.00713 instead of 521 and 1680. Both carry units of Hz-1, so κ·f must be O(1) — a dimensional sniff test that was skipped. The high-frequency cutoff vanished and the foreground stayed 7.9×105 too high at 10 mHz. Worse: the validation gate's window ended at 5 mHz, right before the bug became visible. Both were fixed; the gate now checks that the foreground is invisible at 10 mHz, which any public LISA plot shows.

The arm-length argument, stated backwards

The design doc originally argued "shot-noise-limited strain is independent of arm length, so longer arms buy nothing at high frequency." The algebra is right — but this design is not shot-noise limited: the length-independent noise floor (5.69 pm) exceeds shot noise (4.85 pm), so h ∝ 1/L holds and longer arms pay everywhere. The best argument for the chosen 3 Gm had been written as an argument against it. The plot's own caption contradicted its own curves, 12× apart, on the same page.

102% error with a perfect twin next to it

The FEM's relative mirror decenter missed the exact analytic value by 102% while the relative tilt matched to 0.03%. Fingerprint of a frame-invariance bug: u(M2)−u(M1) is not invariant under the rigid-body rotation that the solver's motion suppression injects — the tilt difference is. Correcting to the M1-frame quantity, dDec = (u₂−u₁) + tilt₁·z₂, landed on the analytic answer to 0.04%. One quantity right and its sibling wrong is diagnostic gold.

Six lasers all pointing at the centroid

First render of the formation exhibit: every beam converged on the triangle's centre — too tidy to be random. The aperture-lookup function used two scratch vectors internally while its callers used the same two vectors to hold both endpoints; the second call overwrote the first result with a unit vector near the origin. Shared mutable scratch versus output containers. Suspiciously regular wrongness is a shared-state signature.

07

Try it

Both exhibits are live city assets with bilingual knowledge cards.

Open the viewer with viewer/index.html?colony=1&inspect=tt1-formation-01 or walk to the science quarter around (-430,-150). Eleven POI cards (EN/中文 toggle in the viewer) carry the same ledger numbers as this page — 651 pW, 2.10 fm/s²/√Hz, 220 µK/√Hz all resolve to the runs listed above.

Things worth catching: the gold cube behind the cutaway wall of the 1:1 spacecraft; the beams landing exactly on the telescope apertures while the triangle breathes (watch ~36 s for a full baked year); the MGA gimbal — deliberately the only moving part, because a drag-free platform tolerates no reaction wheels; and the spec plaque's claim that the whole thermal design collapses to one line: 2×10-4 K/√Hz along the metering path.
